lesson.title: Trust No One, Verify Everyone: Zero Trust Networking
lesson.summary: Zero trust networking abandons the assumption that being inside the network perimeter means being trustworthy, instead requiring every request to be authenticated and authorized on its own merits, using tools like TLS.
lesson.body:
Zero trust networking is built on a simple refusal: never grant a request implicit trust just because it appears to come from inside the network. Every request, regardless of where it originates, has to be verified and authorized on its own terms before it is allowed through.

The traditional alternative is often described as the castle and moat model, where a strong perimeter, like a firewall, is treated as the boundary between an untrusted outside and a trusted inside, and anything already inside the walls is largely taken at its word. The ARP spoofing chapter is a direct illustration of why that assumption is dangerous: an attacker who is already on the local network, whether by physically connecting to it, joining its Wi-Fi, or compromising one internal device, can exploit exactly the kind of implicit trust that the castle and moat model hands out for free once you are inside. Zero trust responds to this by removing network location as a stand in for trustworthiness altogether.

Zero trust is best understood as a specific application of defense in depth's central lesson, that no single control should carry all the weight. Defense in depth says do not rely on one layer, such as a perimeter firewall, to protect everything behind it. Zero trust takes that lesson and applies it specifically to the question of trust and network location, insisting that every request be checked again rather than being waved through because it originated somewhere presumed safe.

Making that work in practice requires a way to authenticate and encrypt communication between any two points on the network, not just at the perimeter, and this is exactly where TLS comes in. TLS provides per connection encryption along with certificate based identity, so that even traffic between two devices on the same internal network must present valid credentials and travels encrypted rather than in the clear. That directly closes off the kind of silent interception that ARP spoofing enables on an unprotected local network, since even if an attacker successfully repositions themselves as a man in the middle, they are met with encrypted, authenticated traffic rather than plaintext.

As a concrete example, consider an employee's laptop on the corporate Wi-Fi requesting an internal human resources service. Under the castle and moat model, simply being connected to that Wi-Fi would often be treated as sufficient proof of legitimacy. Under zero trust, the laptop and the service instead perform mutual authentication over TLS, and the request is checked against policy, who is asking, from what device, for what data, every single time, whether the laptop is sitting in the office or connecting from somewhere else entirely. Network location stops being a credential, and verification becomes the constant instead.
